title: Fizz Buzz Multithreaded
statement:
On LeetCode this is a multithreading problem. Here each thread is an asynchronous task, and you coordinate the tasks with promises.

Write a class `FizzBuzz` whose constructor takes `n`. One shared instance is handed to four threads, which call `fizz(printFizz)`, `buzz(printBuzz)`, `fizzbuzz(printFizzBuzz)` and `number(printNumber)`, one method each. `printFizz()`, `printBuzz()` and `printFizzBuzz()` print the words `"fizz"`, `"buzz"` and `"fizzbuzz"`, and `printNumber(x)` prints the integer `x`. Between them the threads must print one token for each `i` from 1 to `n`, in increasing order of `i`:

- `"fizzbuzz"` when `i` is divisible by both 3 and 5,
- `"fizz"` when `i` is divisible by 3 but not by 5,
- `"buzz"` when `i` is divisible by 5 but not by 3,
- the number `i` itself when it is divisible by neither.

Each method prints only its own kind of token (`number` prints exactly the plain integers) and keeps going until all of its tokens are out, so make the methods `async` and `await` promises between prints.

Each case gives `n`, `threads` and `starts`: thread `i` starts at `starts[i]` ms and calls the method named `threads[i]`. Threads with the same start time start in index order. The answer is `{ output, times }`: the printed tokens in order (words as strings, numbers as numbers) and the time in ms of each print. A token must be printed as soon as it is allowed, that is, once its thread has started and the token before it has been printed, so wait on promises rather than on timers.
signature: Object FizzBuzz(int n, String[] threads, int[] starts)
api: class FizzBuzz { constructor(n: number); fizz(printFizz: () => void): void | Promise<void>; buzz(printBuzz: () => void): void | Promise<void>; fizzbuzz(printFizzBuzz: () => void): void | Promise<void>; number(printNumber: (x: number) => void): void | Promise<void> }
notes:
## Intuition

At every moment exactly one number `i` is due, and exactly one thread owns it: the `fizzbuzz` thread for multiples of 15, `fizz` for other multiples of 3, `buzz` for other multiples of 5 and `number` for the rest. Each thread can list its own numbers in advance, so it only needs to know when its next number becomes due. Keep a shared counter `current`; a thread whose number is not due yet parks a resolve function under that number, and whoever prints `current` moves the counter on and wakes the owner of the new value. (The brute force instead lets whichever thread arrives print every token whose owner has already arrived.)

## Approach

1. Start with `current = 1` and an empty map `waiting` from a number to the resolve function of the thread waiting for it.
2. `waitFor(i)` returns a resolved promise if `i` is already due; otherwise it parks with `waiting.set(i, resolve)`.
3. `advance()` adds 1 to `current` and wakes the thread parked under the new `current`, if any.
4. Each method loops over its own numbers (`fizz`: multiples of 3 that are not multiples of 5, and so on). For each `i` it awaits `waitFor(i)`, prints, then calls `advance()`.

With real threads the usual design is a lock with a condition variable: each thread waits while `current` is not its next number, prints, increments `current` and calls `notifyAll`. Another uses four semaphores, one per thread: after printing `i`, the printer releases the semaphore of the owner of `i + 1`. Parking a resolve function plays the part of waiting, and calling it the part of the signal.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 15`, threads start in the order fizz, buzz, fizzbuzz, number at 0 ms.

- `fizz` waits for 3, `buzz` for 5 and `fizzbuzz` for 15; all three park.
- `number` finds 1 due: it prints 1, advances to 2 and prints 2, advances to 3 and wakes `fizz`, then parks waiting for 4.
- `fizz` prints `"fizz"` and advances to 4, waking `number`; the hand-offs continue the same way up to `"fizzbuzz"` for 15.
- The answer is `[1, 2, "fizz", 4, "buzz", ..., 14, "fizzbuzz"]`, every token at 0 ms.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each number is printed once, with O(1) work to park and wake.
- Space: O(1) besides the map, which holds at most one entry per thread (four).

## Pitfalls

- Checking divisibility by 3 before 15: 15, 30 and 45 must go to `fizzbuzz`, not `fizz`.
- A thread that loops until `current > n` must also be woken at the end, or it never finishes; looping over the thread's own numbers avoids that.
- Waking only after a delay (`setTimeout`) prints late; wait on the promise itself.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `current` | the number whose token must be printed next |
| `waiting` | map from a number to the resolve function of the thread waiting for it |
| `wake` | the resolve function of the owner of the new `current`, if it is waiting |
| `i` | in each method, the next number this thread owns |
